For two weeks now, someone had been leaving marigolds in Aparna's cycle basket outside the Government Girls' School. On the third Sunday at the village mela, she saw who: Gopal from the boys' school across the pond, watching her from behind the balloon stall like she was a film heroine.
Her friend Simran giggled. "He's crazy about you. You could make him do anything."
Aparna felt her cheeks warm. It was nice, being looked at like that. It was also uncomfortable. Gopal didn't know that she bit her nails and failed her Sanskrit test.
On Monday, when he appeared near her cycle again, she said calmly, "Gopal, thank you for the flowers. They're pretty. But I'm just an ordinary girl, not someone in a film. Please don't leave them anymore."
Gopal went red, nodded and walked away fast. Aparna felt a pang, but also lighter.

qa.q: Where did Aparna find the marigolds?
qa.a: In her cycle basket outside the Government Girls' School.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she learned it was Gopal?
qa.a: She felt flattered and warm-cheeked but also uncomfortable, because he saw an idealised version of her.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than Simran's suggestion, and why?
qa.a: Aparna thanked Gopal kindly and asked him to stop, rather than using his feelings for power, which respected both of them.

qa.q: How might Gopal feel after Aparna speaks to him?
qa.a: Gopal probably feels embarrassed and disappointed, but she was kind, so he can walk away with his dignity.

grounding: A teen idolised by a boy feels flattered and uneasy, reminds him kindly that she is ordinary, and sets a boundary.

In Class 10, I told Nivedita I liked her. I'd practised it for a week. She was kind, but the answer was no. She liked someone else.
I didn't sleep that night. It felt like a punch in the chest that kept happening.
The next day I wanted to do a lot of stupid things. Message her again with a longer explanation. Tell people she'd led me on, which wasn't even true. Some of the boys in my class were already saying, "She thinks she's too good for you, Tushar."
My best friend Eshaan stopped that. "She said no politely. Don't make her a villain," he said, and then he took me for kulfi and let me talk for an hour.
I let myself be sad for a few weeks. I didn't pester her. And I learned something: I could survive a no. That felt oddly like strength.

qa.a: That she liked someone else.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel the night after the rejection?
qa.a: Tushar felt badly hurt, like a punch in the chest that kept happening, and could not sleep.

qa.q: Which choices helped Tushar get through the rejection?

After basketball practice, in the empty sports hall, Farah caught up with Jeevan. "Can I say something? I really like you. Like, like you."
Jeevan's stomach dropped. He liked Farah as a teammate, a good one. Nothing more.
Tushar had told him on Monday, "If she asks, just say maybe. Keep her around. It's nice being liked."
Jeevan took a breath. "Farah, thank you for telling me. That took guts. But I don't feel the same way. I'm sorry."
Farah's face fell. "Okay. That's clear."
"I still want to pass to you in the match on Friday," he said. "You're our best shooter."
She laughed shakily. "Obviously."

Eshaan, you keep hiding when that girl from your tuition walks past. Sit. I was exactly the same.
In Class 9 in Lucknow, there was Shabnam, who sat by the window. Whenever she came near, my tongue turned to wood. I'd lie in bed imagining every way I might embarrass myself: dropping my books, saying something stupid, my voice cracking.
My plan was to write her a long, dramatic letter and give it to her on the last day of school. Thank God I never did.
The turning point was a pencil. One day hers broke in the exam hall, and before I could think, I held mine out. She said, "Thanks, Raghav," and smiled.
The next day I said, "Did the pencil survive?" It was a ridiculous line. She laughed anyway.
After that we talked about ordinary things: exams, cricket, rain. Awkward, yes, but that's normal. Start with a pencil, beta.

Her mind raced. Say something smart. No, you'll stutter. Your hair looks like a wet mop. He'll think you're weird.
She stared at the rain and said nothing for five whole minutes.
Her phone buzzed. Lavanya, her best friend: "Is that AMAN next to u?? just say hi. normal hi."
Mehak took a breath. "The bus is always late when it rains," she said. Her voice came out a little squeaky.
Aman grinned. "Always. Once I waited an hour and missed my own birthday cake."
Mehak laughed, the awkwardness still there but smaller. By the time the bus came, they'd talked about the science fair, and she hadn't died of embarrassment even once.

Ishita's friend Neelam brought her to my office during lunch. Ishita was quiet at first, turning her phone over and over.
She told me her boyfriend, Karan, checks her messages every evening and has her passwords. He tells her which clothes are "okay" and gets very angry when she spends time with friends. She said, "He does it because he loves me, right?"
I said clearly that checking her phone, choosing her clothes and cutting her off from friends is control, not a proof of love, and that none of it is her fault. She cried, then seemed relieved.
We made a plan together: she will change her passwords today, keep Neelam and her other friends close, and she agreed I could phone her mother this afternoon. I called her mother at 3 p.m.; she is coming in tomorrow morning. I will check in with Ishita before she leaves school today.

When I was with Vivek, I felt like I couldn't breathe without him. That's what I told myself was love.
I needed him to text me every hour. If he didn't reply in ten minutes, my heart pounded and I imagined he'd stopped caring. I asked him to share his location "just so I know you're okay." I checked who he'd followed. At night I'd ask, "Do you still love me?" three, four times.

I stopped asking for his location. I joined the badminton club again. Some days are still hard. But I can breathe on my own now.

Football coach's note, under-17 squad, Tuesday
Over the past month, Jeevan's focus in training has dropped. He checks his phone between every drill. Today he left the pitch twice to text, and when he came back he was pale.
His teammate Darshan told me Jeevan messages his girlfriend, Mitali, almost every few minutes, and gets upset if she doesn't reply straight away. Darshan said Jeevan once asked him to check who Mitali was chatting with in the canteen, and Darshan refused.
After training I sat with Jeevan on the bench. He admitted, "If I don't know where she is, I feel like I'm going to fall apart." I told him that sounds like anxiety, not love, and that watching her would hurt them both.
He agreed to see the school counsellor. I walked him to the counsellor's office before he went home today. I'll also give him back a leadership role in drills, so he has something of his own to focus on.

qa.a: To check who Mitali was chatting with in the canteen.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel when he doesn't know where Mitali is?
qa.a: He feels anxious and panicky, as if he is going to fall apart.

qa.q: How did the coach support Jeevan wisely?
qa.a: By naming the feelings as anxiety not love, saying monitoring would hurt them both, walking him to the counsellor the same day and giving him a role of his own.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Jeevan's behaviour?
qa.a: Darshan seems worried and uncomfortable, refusing to help watch Mitali and telling the coach because he cares about Jeevan.

grounding: A coach observes a teen who needs constant check-ins from his girlfriend, names it as anxiety, and connects him with support.
